This is what renting stability looks like.

Egypt just held its benchmark rate at 19% for the fourth straight meeting, with inflation at 14.9%, one of the highest real interest rates on the planet. It froze an almost yearlong rate-cutting cycle the moment the Iran war put fresh pressure on the pound and its fuel-import bill.

Those real yields are bait. Foreign money piles into Egyptian local debt to collect the carry, and that hot money helps hold the pound together. But Egypt still cannot stand on its own, surviving on an $8 billion IMF program and a €4 billion EU lifeline.

A carry trade pays this much because the currency underneath it can break. If the war escalates or global risk turns, the foreign money leaves first, and a pound propped up by 19% rates and IMF cash cracks fast.
